decision_reason: Preserve the nine A1 concepts and add one wrist-scoped gravity-relative reorientation attribute. Eating soup and drinking from cup are the closest unseen pair, differing only in rotational_motion and motion_regularity; distinguishing orientation excursion from overall rotation provides a plausible additional contrast between comparatively level utensil transport and cup tipping. Seen utensil-use and object-handling activities provide transfer anchors, although execution variability limits this distinction. Other close pairs, especially sitting versus standing, do not justify additional attributes without stronger assumptions about phone placement or body configuration. The relatively weak coverage of jogging, kicking (soccer ball), and clapping does not by itself justify speculative new dimensions.

attributes.name: motion_intensity
attributes.definition: Overall magnitude and energy of motion within a window, including both linear and rotational components.

attributes.name: cadence
attributes.definition: Rate at which a meaningful periodic motion unit repeats over time. Cadence measures repetitions per unit time, not the total number of repetitions in the recording.

levels.Low: No clear periodic repetition or a slow repetition rate.

attributes.name: smoothness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion changes continuously rather than through sustained rapid fluctuations.

levels.Medium: Moderately smooth motion with some fluctuations.
levels.High: Continuous and smooth motion with little fluctuation.

attributes.name: impulsiveness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion contains short, abrupt, high-magnitude changes or impacts.

levels.Low: Few or no pronounced abrupt peaks.

attributes.name: posture_inclination
attributes.definition: Average gravity-relative inclination of the global load-bearing body configuration within a window, rather than the orientation of an isolated moving limb.

levels.High: Strongly inclined or nearly horizontal relative to gravity.

attributes.name: posture_variability
attributes.definition: Extent to which the global load-bearing body configuration changes relative to gravity within a window, rather than local limb-orientation changes.

attributes.name: rotational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of angular or rotational motion during the activity.

attributes.name: translational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of sustained linear progression or locomotor translation within a window.

levels.High: Prominent sustained translational or locomotor motion.

attributes.name: motion_regularity
attributes.definition: Temporal consistency and predictability of the motion pattern.

levels.Low: Irregular and poorly predictable motion pattern.
levels.Medium: Partly structured motion with moderate variability.

attributes.name: wrist_tilt_excursion
attributes.definition: Extent of change in the wrist-worn watch's orientation relative to gravity during an activity window, excluding rotation that leaves its gravity-relative orientation unchanged.

levels.Low: Wrist orientation relative to gravity remains nearly constant.
levels.Medium: Wrist orientation relative to gravity changes through a moderate range.
levels.High: Wrist orientation relative to gravity changes through a large range.

operations.reason: motion_intensity: G3 supports differences in acceleration and angular-motion energy, retaining transferable contrasts between vigorous unseen activities and quieter seen activities. Speed, effort, and phone placement can change observed magnitude; intensity alone does not identify the activity.

cadence: G6 supports repetition-rate evidence from recurring inertial motion. It transfers locomotor and repetitive-action structure without equating repetition speed with energy. Irregular bouts, pauses, and multiple motion timescales can make the meaningful repetition unit ambiguous.

smoothness: G9 supports sustained rapid-change evidence, preserving the existing soup-versus-sandwich contrast and the distinction between continuous handling and repeated abrupt motion. Execution speed and sensor movement can affect apparent smoothness; this is not an isolated-impact measure.

impulsiveness: G10 supports brief rapid-change peaks, transferring impact-like structure from seen ball activities to clapping, kicking, and jogging. A wrist or carried phone may attenuate distant foot impacts, and abrupt voluntary movements can resemble contact events; no contact identity is inferred.

posture_inclination: G1 supports gravity-relative orientation in principle, retaining the existing sitting-versus-standing distinction. Global posture is only indirectly observable when the carried phone follows the load-bearing body; wrist orientation is not a substitute. Sitting can also be upright, so the A1 contrast is not a universal biomechanical rule and no stronger posture distinction is added.

posture_variability: G12 supports changing gravity-relative body orientation when phone motion reflects the body. This preserves a balance-and-body-adjustment contrast for kicking relative to quieter or more localized actions. Loose carriage and isolated wrist movement can mimic posture change, limiting inference about the global configuration.

rotational_motion: G2 supports angular-motion prominence, preserving the existing soup-versus-cup distinction and transfer from seen rotational handling. Angular activity can occur without substantial gravity-relative tilt, so this remains distinct from wrist_tilt_excursion. Grip, joint strategy, and movement speed introduce ambiguity.

translational_motion: G13 supports short-window translation proxies, preserving progression as distinct from vigorous stationary movement. Walking and stairs anchor jogging, while catch anchors comparatively localized ball handling. Sustained progression is only indirectly supported by inertial proxies; limb swings and intermittent steps can resemble translation.

motion_regularity: G11 supports recurrence and predictability, retaining temporal organization independently of repetition speed. Seen rhythmic and irregular actions provide anchors for jogging, clapping, and kicking. Short windows and pauses may obscure structure; nearly static signals can be regular without having a meaningful cadence.

wrist_tilt_excursion: G12 supports gravity-relative orientation variation at the available wrist-worn watch, with G2 providing complementary evidence of reorientation. Cup tipping can produce a larger wrist tilt excursion than comparatively level spoon transport, adding a physically different contrast to the close unseen soup–cup pair. Seen eating pasta, writing, and folding clothes provide examples of constrained versus broader wrist reorientation rather than a cup-specific label. Predictability is conditional: the watch must be on the active wrist, spoon lifting can also tilt the wrist, cup grip can reduce tilt, and windows may omit the tipping phase. This is a plausible additional distinction, not guaranteed separation.

semantic_redundancy_review: All 153 activity pairs were considered, with emphasis on the one-coordinate soup–sandwich, soup–writing, and sitting–standing contrasts and the two-coordinate unseen soup–cup contrast. No unsupported hand-shape, utensil-identity, foot-contact, or bilateral-coordination attributes are added. Wrist tilt excursion measures local orientation range, unlike global posture variability or overall angular-motion prominence; rotations about gravity need not increase it. Smoothness concerns sustained fluctuation, whereas impulsiveness concerns brief peaks. Cadence concerns repetition rate, whereas regularity concerns predictability. Some correlations are expected, but the concepts are physically distinct. Close pairs remain unresolved where additional distinctions would depend on unobserved execution details or uncertain phone placement.

_meta.validation: Semantic schema and complete A1-to-A2 lineage validated; no feature binding performed.
